When Credentials Are No Longer Enough: Device Trust in the AI Era

AI is making credential theft, phishing, and MFA bypass attempts faster and more convincing, weakening traditional login trust signals like passwords, IP reputation, and geolocation. The article argues that organizations should add device trust so valid credentials alone are not enough to access sensitive systems.
KEY POINTS
  • 01AI has not created a fundamentally new form of account takeover, but it reduces the manual work needed for phishing, credential theft, MFA abuse, session hijacking, and social engineering.
  • 02Traditional trust signals such as passwords, MFA responses, IP reputation, geolocation, and browser characteristics are becoming easier for attackers to steal, imitate, or work around.
  • 03Attackers can route traffic through residential proxies, mobile networks, or compromised systems and choose exit nodes close to victims, making malicious logins appear geographically plausible.
  • 04The article argues that device trust can make valid credentials insufficient by tying access to approved hardware and treating logins from unknown devices as a meaningful change in risk.
  • 05The article says access should continue to depend on both the user’s identity and the health of the device, with enforcement matched to the level of risk and self-guided remediation for users.

Identity security is under pressure because attackers are getting better at stealing, imitating, or bypassing signals such as passwords, MFA responses, IP reputation, geolocation, and browser characteristics. The article says AI has not created a new type of account takeover, but it has made familiar attacks faster and more efficient. Attackers can use AI to generate convincing phishing emails, personalize messages with public information, and focus on accounts with the highest expected value.

Traditional login checks are described as increasingly limited because credentials can come from breaches or infostealer dumps, MFA can be phished or bypassed through stolen session cookies, and network signals can be misleading. Attackers can use residential proxies, mobile networks, or compromised systems to make a login appear geographically plausible. The article cites NIST Zero Trust Architecture guidance that organizations should not grant implicit trust based only on physical or network location.

The article argues that device trust adds another layer by making valid credentials insufficient without the device context they are meant to be used from. It says organizations should tie access to approved hardware, continuously evaluate both the user and device, and adjust enforcement based on the level of risk. It also says users need a clear self-guided way to restore trust when device health issues affect access.

  • The article frames AI’s main impact on account takeover as reducing the cost of personalization and triage, which lets attackers run more campaigns and concentrate effort on higher-value accounts rather than fully automating intrusions.
  • Device trust is presented as a way to reduce reliance on network clues because attackers can make malicious logins look geographically plausible by using residential proxies, mobile networks, or compromised systems near the victim.
  • The article recommends proportionate device enforcement, where a missing update might trigger reduced privileges or a grace period while more serious issues such as disabled endpoint protection or a rooted device can be treated more severely.
  • Self-guided remediation is highlighted as part of device trust because users need a clear way to restore access when their device health blocks or limits them.

The article says attackers are using AI to make stolen-password and fake-login attempts faster, more convincing, and harder to spot, while common clues like location or internet address are less reliable. This affects organizations whose employees use passwords, login prompts, and company or personal devices to access work systems. The stakes are that even a correct password and approval prompt may no longer prove the real employee is logging in, so companies may need to check whether the device itself is trusted and healthy before allowing access.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is sponsored, evergreen guidance about AI-enabled account takeover and device trust rather than reporting a specific incident, vulnerability, patch, or threat actor operation. It may be useful background, but it is low priority for security professionals tracking urgent or concrete developments.

Valve notifies Steam hardware customers of a data breach

Valve is warning European Steam hardware customers that their delivery-related personal data was likely stolen after attackers breached shipping partner CEVA Logistics. Exposed details include names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, and order type/price, but not Steam passwords, payment data, or Steam Guard codes.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Valve is notifying Steam hardware customers in Europe that hackers stole their data after breaching its shipping partner, CEVA Logistics.
  • 02Valve said the attackers had access to CEVA Logistics' servers between July 29 and August 1, 2026, and likely accessed information needed to ship hardware orders to Steam customers.
  • 03The stolen data includes affected customers' names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and the type and price of ordered products.
  • 04Valve said CEVA does not have access to payment information, passwords, Steam Guard codes, or other sensitive Steam account data.
  • 05Valve warned affected customers that they may be targeted by email, SMS, or voice phishing messages impersonating Steam, Valve, or delivery companies.

Valve is notifying Steam hardware customers in Europe that their data was stolen after hackers breached its shipping partner, CEVA Logistics. Valve said the attackers had access to CEVA Logistics’ servers between July 29 and August 1, 2026. Valve learned on August 7 that certain information about Steam customers was likely compromised.

The stolen data includes names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and the type and price of ordered products. Valve said no Steam account information or other purchases were impacted because CEVA does not have access to payment information, passwords, Steam Guard codes, or other sensitive data. CEVA receives specific delivery-related information from Steam so it can ship physical hardware to customers in Europe and retains that information for up to 90 days after an order.

Valve warned affected customers that they may receive phishing messages by email, SMS, or voice that impersonate Steam, Valve, or delivery companies. The company said such messages may quote an address to seem genuine or ask users to confirm a delivery, pay a small fee, or sign in somewhere to verify an order. Valve also said it is pressing CEVA for the full scope of what was taken and is notifying data protection authorities in affected countries.

  • Valve is notifying all customers it can assume were impacted because CEVA Logistics keeps delivery-related Steam hardware information for up to 90 days after an order.
  • The most immediate risk for affected customers is convincing phishing, because attackers may use stolen addresses and order details to make fake delivery or Steam messages appear legitimate.
  • Valve specifically told affected customers they do not need to change their Steam password or account settings because CEVA did not have access to Steam passwords, payment information, Steam Guard codes, or other sensitive account data.
  • The CEVA Logistics incident affected more than Valve, as CEVA had already informed multiple European retailers that the cyberattack disrupted operations at eight European warehouses.

Valve is telling Steam hardware customers in Europe that some of their delivery information was likely stolen after hackers broke into CEVA Logistics, the company that ships Valve’s hardware there. The affected information includes names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and the type and price of products ordered, but not Steam passwords, payment details, or Steam Guard codes. This matters because scammers may use the stolen details to send convincing messages pretending to be Steam, Valve, or a delivery company and ask people to pay fees or sign in somewhere fake.

New StormEncryptor ransomware used by former Medusa affiliate

Microsoft says China-based threat actor Storm-1175, formerly linked to Medusa ransomware, is now deploying a new ransomware strain called StormEncryptor after likely exploiting an N-able N-central authentication-bypass flaw. Admins of self-hosted N-central servers should urgently apply the August hotfix and check for compromise because the group moves from initial access to data theft and encryption within days.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft Threat Intelligence says the financially motivated threat actor Storm-1175, previously associated with Medusa ransomware, is now deploying a new ransomware strain called StormEncryptor.
  • 02Microsoft says the recent attacks were likely preceded by exploitation of CVE-2026-18577, an authentication-bypass vulnerability in N-able’s N-central remote monitoring and management tool.
  • 03StormEncryptor is a C++ malware that appends encrypted files with the “.encrypted” extension and drops a ransom note named “!!!README_FIRST!!!.txt” into every scanned directory.
  • 04After gaining access to target networks, the attacker used AnyDesk or SimpleHelp for remote management, Advanced IP Scanner for network discovery, and Mimikatz to dump credentials from the LSASS process.
  • 05N-able released hotfix 2026.3 HF1/build 2026.3.1.7 on August 2 and urged customers to install it immediately.

A financially motivated threat actor previously associated with the Medusa ransomware operation is now deploying a new ransomware strain called StormEncryptor. Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks the actor as Storm-1175 and says the recent attacks were likely preceded by exploitation of CVE-2026-18577, an authentication-bypass vulnerability in N-able’s N-central remote monitoring and management tool. Microsoft says Storm-1175 is believed to be China-based and was previously linked to attacks involving zero-day and n-day flaws in products including GoAnywhere MFT, SmarterTools SmarterMail, Microsoft Exchange, Ivanti Connect Secure, and JetBrains TeamCity.

Microsoft says Storm-1175’s deployment of StormEncryptor is the actor’s first activity it has observed since April 2026 and represents a shift away from Medusa ransomware. StormEncryptor is described as C++ malware that appends encrypted files with the “.encrypted” extension and drops a ransom note named “!!!README_FIRST!!!.txt” into every scanned directory. The ransom note gives victims three days to contact the attacker and negotiate payment, or stolen data will be leaked online.

After gaining access to target networks, the attacker used AnyDesk or SimpleHelp for remote management, Advanced IP Scanner for network discovery, and Mimikatz to dump credentials from the LSASS process. Microsoft warned that Storm-1175 can move from initial access to data exfiltration and ransomware deployment within a few days, and urged organizations to monitor for the actor’s activity and apply security patches as soon as possible. N-able released hotfix 2026.3 HF1/build 2026.3.1.7 on August 2 for CVE-2026-18577 and previously recommended checks for signs of compromise such as an svchost.exe file in users’ Documents folders, a Cloudflared service, and inbound connections from IP addresses listed in its advisory.

  • Storm-1175’s use of StormEncryptor is notable because Microsoft says it is the actor’s first observed activity since April 2026 and marks a shift away from the Medusa ransomware it previously used.
  • The article highlights self-hosted N-central servers as an urgent priority because Microsoft says Storm-1175 can move from initial access to data theft and ransomware deployment within a few days.
  • N-able’s compromise checks give defenders concrete indicators to look for, including an svchost.exe file in users’ Documents folders, a Cloudflared service, and inbound connections from IP addresses listed in its advisory.
  • StormEncryptor’s ransom note combines file encryption with a data-leak threat, giving victims three days to contact the attackers before stolen data is leaked online.

Microsoft says a China-based criminal group that used to work with the Medusa ransomware operation is now using a new program called StormEncryptor to lock victims’ files and demand payment. The attacks likely began by abusing a security flaw in N-able’s N-central remote management tool, which is used by administrators to manage computers. Organizations running their own N-central servers are most directly affected and are urged to install N-able’s fix right away. This matters because the group can move from breaking in to stealing data and locking systems within just a few days, then threaten to leak stolen information if victims do not pay.

Critical Progress LoadMaster flaw now actively exploited in attacks

CISA says attackers are actively exploiting a critical unauthenticated command injection flaw in Progress Kemp LoadMaster, and federal agencies have been ordered to patch within three days. All organizations using affected LoadMaster or MOVEit WAF versions should update immediately to block remote command execution attacks.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CISA warned that hackers are exploiting CVE-2026-8037, a critical Progress Kemp LoadMaster command injection vulnerability.
  • 02CVE-2026-8037 allows unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary commands on unpatched LoadMaster appliances by exploiting unsanitized API inputs in multiple command endpoints.
  • 03Progress Software released security updates in June for affected Kemp LoadMaster versions and confirmed the flaw also impacts all MOVEit WAF versions before GA v7.2.63.2.
  • 04Shadowserver reported nearly 300 Kemp LoadMaster instances exposed online, though it is unknown how many are honeypots or already secured against CVE-2026-8037.
  • 05CISA added CVE-2026-8037 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and ordered U.S. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies to secure affected servers within three days.

CISA warned that hackers are exploiting CVE-2026-8037, a critical command injection vulnerability in Progress Kemp LoadMaster. Kemp LoadMaster is an Application Delivery Controller and server load balancer used by technology companies and government entities worldwide to distribute web traffic, optimize application performance, and maintain availability. Progress Software says 80% of Fortune 500 companies use its products and services, and that Kemp LoadMaster has over 100,000 deployments worldwide.

The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary commands on unpatched LoadMaster appliances by exploiting unsanitized API inputs in multiple command endpoints. Progress released security updates in June for Kemp LoadMaster GA v7.2.63.1 or older and LTSF v7.2.54.17 or older. The company also confirmed that all MOVEit WAF versions before GA v7.2.63.2 are affected.

Shadowserver reported nearly 300 Kemp LoadMaster instances exposed online, though the article says it is unclear how many are honeypots or already protected against CVE-2026-8037. CISA added the flaw to its catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities and ordered U.S. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies to secure their servers within three days under Binding Operational Directive 26-04. CISA said this type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise, while also urging all defenders to prioritize patching.

  • CISA’s three-day deadline for federal agencies indicates the agency views CVE-2026-8037 as requiring unusually urgent remediation once exploitation is confirmed.
  • The vulnerability affects both Kemp LoadMaster and MOVEit WAF, so organizations should not limit their checks to LoadMaster deployments alone.
  • Progress patched the flaw in June, but CISA’s later warning shows that systems remaining unpatched after the update became active targets.
  • Shadowserver’s count of nearly 300 internet-exposed LoadMaster instances may overstate or understate real risk because the article notes it is unknown how many are honeypots or already secured.

U.S. officials warned that hackers are actively abusing a serious flaw in Progress Kemp LoadMaster, a product used by many companies and government groups to spread website traffic across servers and keep services available. Progress says its products are used by 80% of Fortune 500 companies, and LoadMaster has over 100,000 deployments worldwide, so the issue could affect many organizations if they have not installed the June fixes. The flaw can let outsiders run commands on unpatched systems without logging in, which is why federal agencies were ordered to secure their servers quickly and all other users were urged to do the same.

BdThemes plugins supply-chain hack creates rogue WordPress admins

BdThemes’ WordPress plugin ecosystem was hit by a supply-chain compromise where attackers poisoned a remote JSON feed to run malicious JavaScript in admin dashboards, creating hidden rogue administrator accounts. Affected plugins were pulled from WordPress.org while the issue remained under investigation.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A threat actor compromised BdThemes’ upstream infrastructure and modified a remote JSON feed delivered to administrators’ browsers to create rogue WordPress administrator accounts.
  • 02Wordfence researchers said the attacker poisoned a static remote JSON data stream after obtaining write access to the vendor’s storage bucket, exploiting a cross-site scripting flaw in the Biggop Library used by the Biggopti component.
  • 03The malicious JavaScript used a legitimate administrator’s authenticated session to create rogue admin accounts, and an additional payload called w2.js established persistence through a webshell named emer-run.php by installing a fake plugin.
  • 04The affected BdThemes plugins were pulled from the WordPress.org directory on August 8 pending investigation, and the issue was listed as unpatched as of publication.
  • 05Defiant said the earliest possible start of the campaign was June 23, while Wordfence began seeing attacks through its web application firewall on August 7.

A threat actor compromised the upstream infrastructure of BdThemes, a developer of premium WordPress web-design tools, and modified a remote JSON feed delivered to administrators’ browsers to create rogue admin accounts. BdThemes provides plugins including Element Pack, Prime Slider, Ultimate Post Kit, Pixel Gallery, and Ultimate Store Kit. Its free Element Pack plugin shows more than 100,000 active installations on WordPress.org, while BdThemes advertises more than 350,000 active installs across its portfolio.

Defiant said Wordfence began seeing attacks through its web application firewall on August 7, and researchers determined the earliest possible start of the campaign was June 23. The affected BdThemes products were pulled from the WordPress.org directory on August 8 pending investigation, and the article says the issue was listed as unpatched as of publication. At the time of writing, BdThemes had not published an official statement, and BleepingComputer had not received a response to its request for comment.

Researchers said the attacker poisoned a static remote JSON data stream after obtaining write access to the vendor’s storage bucket. The attack exploited a cross-site scripting flaw in the Biggop Library used by the Biggopti component, allowing malicious JavaScript to run when a logged-in administrator opened a wp-admin page. Sens. Adam Schiff and Amy Klobuchar introduced the Water Cyber Shield Act, legislation that would allocate $300 million each year for cybersecurity improvements in the U.S. water and wastewater sector. The bill would give the Environmental Protection Agency increased authority to regulate cybersecurity protections for water and wastewater systems. It follows recent cyberattacks on at least 30 water and wastewater systems in about 12 states, which experts believe were launched by groups connected to Iran’s military.

The legislation would authorize $300 million annually from Drinking Water and Clean Water State Revolving Funds dedicated to cybersecurity improvements. It would amend the Safe Drinking Water Act and the Clean Water Act to allow the EPA to conduct cybersecurity assessments and require corrective actions when vulnerabilities are found. Water and wastewater systems would also need to assess cybersecurity risk as part of resilience planning and comply with incident reporting requirements under the forthcoming Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act.

The act would set different rules based on the size of water systems and allow states to decide whether to handle the cybersecurity regulations themselves or ask the EPA to help. The EPA would coordinate with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency on threat information and cybersecurity standards, with a technical advisory committee created to develop those standards. Cybersecurity information submitted by utilities would be exempt from public disclosure, while smaller systems would receive flexibility and be prioritized for federal financial assistance.

The proposal would also give the Environmental Protection Agency more power to check these systems for weaknesses and require fixes when problems are found. This matters because recent attacks have hit at least 30 water and wastewater systems in about 12 states, forcing some to turn off tools or run systems by hand. New Passkey Attacks Can Recover Synced Private Keys or Bypass Phishing-Resistant MFA

Recent research showed that passkeys can be bypassed or abused when surrounding systems expose signed authentication data, mishandle synced key protection, or allow malware in an active Windows session to use hardware-backed credentials. The core cryptography remains intact, but defenders should patch Windows, harden WebAuthn validation, and treat endpoints and passkey stores as high-value credential targets.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Three separate research efforts demonstrated ways to defeat passkey protections without breaking the cryptography behind them.
  • 02SpecterOps showed a Windows and Microsoft Entra ID chain that reused signed authentication material exposed by Windows to impersonate privileged users while satisfying phishing-resistant multifactor authentication.
  • 03Unit 42 showed attacks against Google Password Manager in Chrome on Windows, including a method called Golden Pass-ta-key that can recover private keys for a victim's synced passkeys by targeting the Security Domain Secret.
  • 04Dirk-jan Mollema showed that malware already running in a signed-in Windows session can use a hardware-bound Windows Hello for Business key without prompting the user for a fresh PIN or biometric check.
  • 05Microsoft has issued a security update for CVE-2026-34348 and said it applied mitigations for the reported issue involving passkey relay assertions.

Three separate research efforts demonstrated ways to defeat passkey protections without breaking the cryptography they rely on. SpecterOps showed a Windows and Microsoft Entra ID chain that could impersonate privileged users while satisfying phishing-resistant multifactor authentication by reusing signed authentication material. Unit 42 showed attacks against Google Password Manager in Chrome on Windows, including a path to recover private keys for a victim’s synced passkeys. Dirk-jan Mollema showed that malware already running in a signed-in Windows session can use a hardware-bound Windows Hello for Business key without a fresh PIN or biometric check.

The article emphasizes that the impact and fixes differ across the three cases. Microsoft’s Windows logging vulnerability, CVE-2026-34348, has a vendor CVSS score of 6.5 and a Microsoft security update, and Microsoft said it also applied mitigations for the reported issue involving passkey relay assertions. Unit 42’s most damaging variant, Golden Pass-ta-key, targets the Security Domain Secret, a 32-byte master key used to protect synced passkeys, and the researchers said Google’s current implementation provides no way to rotate or revoke it. Mollema found that an Entra WebAuthn challenge is valid for five minutes and is not bound to a session, user, or tenant, allowing it to be signed on a victim machine and returned as an assertion.

The findings show that neither synced passkeys nor device-bound passkeys remove risk when surrounding systems mishandle authentication material or when an endpoint is already compromised. The article says Unit 42’s and Mollema’s attacks begin with malware or access inside an existing user session, so they show what passkeys may fail to contain after endpoint compromise rather than an unauthenticated remote defeat. Recommended actions include installing Microsoft’s applicable updates for CVE-2026-34348, enforcing requested WebAuthn user-verification requirements, treating passkey stores and browser memory as credential-sensitive, and monitoring unusual Windows Hello for Business authentications without a device identifier and unexpected device registrations.

  • The article emphasizes that choosing between synced and device-bound passkeys does not eliminate the broader risk, because the demonstrated attacks target different surrounding systems rather than the passkey cryptography itself.
  • Unit 42's findings make the Security Domain Secret especially consequential because the article says Google's current implementation provides no way to rotate or revoke it after compromise.
  • Mollema's research shows an actionable monitoring angle for Entra defenders: unusual Windows Hello for Business authentications without a device identifier and unexpected device registrations may indicate abuse.
  • The SpecterOps and Mollema findings both involved Microsoft Entra ID authentication outcomes, but the article cautions that the public material does not establish whether they come from the same underlying Entra validation issue.

Researchers showed three ways that attackers could get around passkey protections without breaking the underlying security math. The problems affect Windows and Microsoft Entra ID users, Google Password Manager in Chrome on Windows, and people using Windows Hello for Business when their computer or signed-in session is already compromised. This matters because passkeys are meant to replace passwords and stop fake-login tricks, but mistakes in the surrounding software can still let attackers sign in as someone else or recover synced passkey keys.

Kaspersky said it detected July 2026 attacks by the threat actor Head Mare that exploited unpatched TrueConf servers used by Russian companies in sectors including instrumentation, electronics, transport, energy, IT, and software development. The attackers used a vulnerability chain in TrueConf Server to replace legitimate TrueConf client installers with poisoned versions containing the PhantomCore backdoor and remote access trojan. The affected TrueConf Server versions include 5.3.x up to 5.3.9, 5.4.x up to 5.4.9, 5.5.x up to 5.5.5, and earlier.

The attack begins with a connection to TCP port 4307, which is open by default, followed by exploitation of KLCERT-26-057 to run a malicious script and KLCERT-26-058 to escape an isolated environment. The attackers then execute code with NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges and replace “…\public\js\locale.php” with a web shell for persistent remote access. Kaspersky said the web shell was used to collect infrastructure data, gain privileged access to the TrueConf database, and swap the original TrueConf Client distribution for the infected one.

The web shell also served as a conduit for PhantomGraph, a backdoor using SysExcSvc.dll and SysReadSvc.dll, with Microsoft OneDrive used for command-and-control storage. The article also describes a separate HelloNet campaign that abuses the ViPNet product suite update mechanism to run HelloInjector, HelloProxy, and related components against Russian government, energy, transport, education, and logistics sectors. TrueConf patched the vulnerabilities in Server versions 5.3.9, 5.4.9, and 5.5.5 released on June 18, 2026, and organizations using TrueConf are advised to install the latest versions.

  • The TrueConf attack turns a trusted software distribution channel into the delivery mechanism, so systems that were not directly exploited could still be infected by downloading the replaced TrueConf Client installer.
  • Head Mare’s TrueConf exploitation path starts through TCP port 4307, which the article says is open by default, making exposed unpatched servers especially actionable targets for remediation.
  • PhantomGraph was split into two DLL modules, and Kaspersky assessed that this was deliberate to make detection by EDR tools harder.
  • The article shows repeated targeting of Russia-focused software supply and update channels, with both TrueConf installers and the ViPNet update mechanism used as entry points in separate campaigns.
  • Although the TrueConf flaws were patched on June 18, 2026, Kaspersky still detected exploitation in July 2026, showing that organizations remaining on older versions were still exposed after fixes became available.

Hackers known as Head Mare broke into unpatched TrueConf video meeting servers used by Russian companies in fields such as energy, transport, IT, electronics, and software development. They used the access to swap legitimate TrueConf client installers for infected ones that could secretly give them control of more computers. This matters because software that people trust to communicate or update their systems can become a way for attackers to spread inside important organizations if it is not kept up to date.

Cybersecurity researchers flagged a malicious Microsoft Visual Studio Code extension named Solidity Pro that delivered a browser wallet and credential stealer. The extensions were named helper-beeps.solidity-pro and web3devtoolsx.solidity-pro, and neither is now available on Open VSX. The GitHub repository for web3devtoolsx/solidity-pro remained accessible at the time of writing.

Yeeth Security reported that early versions from 1.0.0 through 2.4.x contacted Cloudflare Workers endpoints to retrieve and execute an encrypted Python payload. Versions starting with 3.0.0 shifted to a full information stealer that collected browser profiles, crypto wallets, source-control tokens, API keys, SSH keys, and Telegram bot tokens. The captured data was exfiltrated through a Telegram bot upload.

The stealer harvested items including GitHub and GitLab tokens, AWS keys and session tokens, Cloudflare tokens, OpenAI keys, mnemonic and seed phrases, multiple crypto wallet vaults, Bitcoin private key material, SSH private keys, URL credentials, and 1Password MFA tokens. Yeeth Security said the malware used heavy obfuscation, clean intermediate versions, and randomized delayed activation to bypass marketplace review, static scanning, and casual sandboxing. Users who installed the extensions were advised to remove them, inspect dependency graphs, block known command-and-control domains, and alert on use of cscript, mshta, cmd, curl, and powershell commands.

  • Automated extension checks that observe packages only for minutes may miss this activity because the malicious code can wait hours or days before running.
  • Clean intermediate versions were used to build trust before malicious behavior appeared, so relying on an extension’s earlier harmless behavior is not sufficient.
  • Static scanners that focus only on dangerous Node imports can miss abuse of first-party VS Code APIs, such as clipboard access used by another bogus Solidity extension.
  • Although the two extensions are no longer available on Open VSX, the article says the GitHub repository for web3devtoolsx/solidity-pro remained accessible at the time of writing.
  • The recommended response goes beyond uninstalling the extensions and includes inspecting dependency graphs, blocking known command-and-control domains, and alerting on cscript, mshta, cmd, curl, and powershell commands.

Researchers found that two Visual Studio Code add-ons pretending to help Solidity developers were secretly built to steal crypto wallet data, passwords, API keys, source-control tokens, SSH keys, and Telegram bot tokens. The people most affected are developers who installed helper-beeps.solidity-pro or web3devtoolsx.solidity-pro, especially those working with cryptocurrency or software projects. This matters because the stolen information could let attackers take money from wallets or access private code and online accounts, and the add-ons were designed to wait before acting so they could avoid quick checks.

Microsoft disclosed that Storm-1175, a financially motivated threat actor linked to China, has deployed a previously undocumented ransomware strain called StormEncryptor. StormEncryptor is written in C++ and appends the .encrypted file name extension to files it encrypts. It also drops a ransom note named !!!README_FIRST!!!.txt in every scanned directory. CVE-2026-18577 is assessed as a patch bypass for CVE-2026-18556, and both flaws can allow authentication bypass and account takeover in susceptible versions.

Known Sender, Perfect Auth, Confirmed Malicious Link

A fully authenticated vendor CRM reply in a real healthcare service thread was quarantined because it contained a URL independently scored as malicious, showing that SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and sender familiarity do not prove message safety. Release decisions should evaluate the flagged content itself, not rely on known-sender trust.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A logistics coordinator at a regional U.S. healthcare system received a reply to a genuine service request from a long-standing equipment vendor, and the message included the correct case reference and instrument serial numbers.
  • 02The email came from the vendor’s own corporate domain through its CRM sending stream, with SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and Microsoft composite authentication all passing.
  • 03One hyperlink in ordinary paragraph text pointed to hxxps://process[.]to/, which was recorded as malicious by the link scanner and corroborated by an external sandbox score of 66 out of 100.
  • 04The message was quarantined on arrival and two more times on repeat delivery attempts, and three release requests based on the sender being known were all denied.
  • 05The article states that authentication confirms sender identity and message integrity but does not determine whether a URL inside the message is safe.

A logistics coordinator at a regional U.S. healthcare system received a reply to a service request sent a week earlier to a long-standing equipment vendor. The message referenced the correct service case, instrument serial numbers, and a third item the service center had received. It came from the vendor’s own corporate domain through the vendor’s CRM sending stream, with SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and Microsoft composite authentication all passing.

Despite those trust signals, one hyperlink in ordinary paragraph text pointed to hxxps://process[.]to/ and carried a recorded malicious verdict. The article says the link scanner recorded the URL as malicious, and an analyst comment cited an external sandbox analysis with a malicious threat level and a score of 66 out of 100. Microsoft Defender for Office 365 had rewritten the URL through Safe Links, but the destination still received malicious verdicts.

The message was quarantined on arrival and was quarantined twice more on repeat delivery attempts. Three separate release requests were submitted on the grounds that the sender was known, and all three were denied with the malicious-content disposition unchanged. The article emphasizes that authentication confirms sender identity and message integrity, but it does not determine whether a URL inside an authenticated message is safe.

  • The strongest reason users gave for releasing the quarantined email, that it came from a known vendor in a real thread, was unrelated to the actual reason it was blocked: a malicious URL verdict.
  • The article highlights that Safe Links rewriting changed the route of the URL but did not by itself settle whether the destination was safe.
  • The malicious link was embedded across a sentence boundary in ordinary service-desk prose, showing that dangerous links may not appear as obvious buttons or suspicious calls to action.
  • The sending vendor’s role was described as incidental, with no evidence of domain compromise, account compromise, or tenant tampering, which makes the case a content-verdict problem rather than a sender-authentication problem.
  • The article recommends that release workflows require evidence about the specific flagged URL before overturning quarantine, especially when operational pressure makes known-sender requests predictable.

A healthcare logistics worker received what looked like a normal reply from a real equipment vendor about a real service request, including the correct case details and instrument serial numbers. Even though the message truly came through the vendor’s normal sending system, one link inside it was judged malicious, so it was quarantined and three requests to release it were denied. This matters because people may trust messages that come from familiar senders and match real conversations, but a single harmful link can still put an organization at risk.

Agents and the EU Act: Navigating Your Responsibilities

Companies deploying AI agents that EU users can interact with are likely covered by the EU AI Act, even though the Act does not explicitly use the word “agent.” At minimum they must meet Article 50 transparency duties, and higher-risk or model-modifying uses can trigger broader provider and high-risk system obligations.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Companies anywhere in the world that deploy public-facing AI applications reachable by EU citizens may fall within the scope of the EU AI Act.
  • 02Article 50 and the European Commission’s transparency guidelines require deployers of AI agents that interact with people to inform those people that they are interacting with AI.
  • 03Agents that generate or manipulate synthetic text, image, audio, or video content must mark human-perceptible content as AI-generated under Article 50(2).
  • 04The article states that AI agents are treated as AI systems under the EU AI Act, so rules that apply to AI systems can also apply to AI agents.
  • 05Deployers that modify models above the Act’s threshold can become providers with additional obligations, and agents used as safety components or for sensitive or personal information can trigger high-risk system requirements under Chapter III.

The article explains how the EU Artificial Intelligence Act applies to AI agents, even though the word “agent” does not appear in the Act itself. It says companies anywhere in the world that deploy public-facing AI applications reachable by EU citizens may fall within the Act’s scope. The author emphasizes that Article 50 creates minimum transparency duties for companies deploying agents that interact with humans.

The article cites European Commission guidance stating that AI agents are covered by Article 50 when they can interact with the people instructing them or with other natural persons while carrying out tasks such as bookings, correspondence, contract negotiation, or purchases. It gives examples including voice assistants, chatbots, AI hotlines, humanoid robots, AI companions, social media bots, and coding agents. Deployers must inform people that they are interacting with AI, using written, visual, auditory, or verifiable AI identity disclosures as appropriate.

The article also explains that AI agents are treated as AI systems under the Act, so broader AI system rules can apply to them. If a company heavily modifies a model and attaches agents to it, the company may become a provider and face additional obligations under Articles 53, 54, and 55. Agents used as safety components or for activities involving sensitive or personal information can trigger high-risk system requirements under Chapter III, along with Article 50 and possible general-purpose AI obligations depending on whether the model is modified.

  • The absence of the word “agent” from the EU AI Act does not reduce compliance duties, because later European Commission guidance explicitly says AI agents can be covered by Article 50 when they interact with people.
  • A company can move from being only a deployer to also being a provider if it modifies an AI model enough, which changes the applicable obligations from basic transparency duties to additional provider duties under Articles 53, 54, and potentially 55.
  • Simply attaching an agent to a model is not treated as modifying the model, so the article separates agent-building from model modification when determining provider obligations.
  • The article recommends treating systemic-risk model obligations as a default planning assumption because it says contemporary models now exceed the Act’s training-compute threshold.
  • High-risk classification can be triggered by what the agent does, such as acting as a safety component or processing sensitive or personal information, regardless of whether the underlying model was modified.

The article explains that companies using AI agents people in the EU can interact with may have legal duties under the EU AI Act, even though the law does not directly use the word “agent.” It says these companies generally need to tell people when they are dealing with AI, and may face stricter rules if the agent handles sensitive or personal information, is part of a safety-related system, or is built on a heavily changed AI model. This matters because public-facing AI tools used by EU citizens can create real compliance responsibilities for companies anywhere in the world.

Kaspersky’s Q2 2026 mobile threat statistics report covers malware, adware, and potentially unwanted software affecting Android, along with notable Android and iOS threats observed during the quarter. Kaspersky also noted that Creduz samples grew significantly despite low activity in victim telemetry, which it said suggests active iteration before a broader campaign.

Kaspersky highlighted malicious loaders hosted directly on Google Play, including a trojanized PDF reader app that used a fake update request to install the Anatsa banking malware. Another loader, detected in the Cleanova app and several others, sent installation-source telemetry from SDKs to a command-and-control server and received a malicious payload only for certain sources. Kaspersky described this as a way to bypass app store review processes while targeting victims more precisely.

  • Creduz banking Trojan samples increased significantly despite low activity in victim telemetry, which Kaspersky says suggests active development and testing before a broader campaign.

AI Governance Fails Without Identity Intelligence – Part 1

AI governance fails if organizations only oversee models and data while ignoring the human, service, application, and machine identities that build, deploy, modify, and operate them. Identity intelligence is needed to connect actions to accountable actors, detect risky or compromised identities, and secure the full AI ecosystem.
KEY POINTS
  • 01The article argues that many organizations govern AI models, data, use cases, and outputs while failing to govern the identities that create, train, authorize, modify, deploy, and operate AI systems.
  • 02AI governance must cover more than generative AI, because AI also includes classifiers, recommendation engines, predictive models, autonomous systems, computer vision, behavioral analytics, robotics, and other systems that predict, recommend, decide, prioritize, classify, or act.
  • 03Identity intelligence goes beyond traditional identity and access management by connecting identities through attribution and examining relationships, behavior, external exposure, historical activity, privilege, device use, and indicators of compromise.
  • 04Without identity attribution, organizations may retain logs but still lack meaningful traceability when cryptic or indirect identities such as service accounts change AI systems.
  • 05The article states that attackers can reach AI systems through trusted identities such as stolen credentials, compromised service accounts, excessive privileges, exposed API keys, weak workload authentication, and unmonitored administrative access.

The article argues that AI governance has a major blind spot when organizations govern models, data, use cases, outputs, and regulations but fail to govern the identities behind AI systems. It says AI systems are created, trained, authorized, modified, deployed, and operated by people, pipelines, service accounts, applications, data sources, administrators, and increasingly autonomous agents. Because each interaction involves identity, authority, and trust, the article says governance cannot be effective without understanding who controls and accesses AI systems.

The article emphasizes that AI governance must cover more than generative AI, including classifiers, recommendation engines, predictive models, autonomous systems, computer vision, behavioral analytics, robotics, and other systems that predict, recommend, decide, prioritize, classify, or act. It distinguishes identity intelligence from traditional identity and access management by saying identity intelligence connects identities through attribution and examines relationships, behavior, external exposure, historical activity, privilege, device use, and indicators of compromise. This context can show which person owns a service account, which pipelines and models depend on it, whether its credentials have been exposed, and whether it should still be trusted.

The article states that accountability, traceability, and human oversight depend on connecting actions to attributable actors rather than relying on cryptic accounts, department names, or logs alone. It also presents identity as an AI security control, noting that attackers may reach AI systems through stolen credentials, compromised service accounts, excessive privileges, exposed API keys, weak workload authentication, or unmonitored administrative access. The article concludes that the real governance boundary is not the model itself, but the broader ecosystem of identities and authority surrounding the model.

  • A log entry showing that a service account changed an AI model has limited governance value unless it is tied to an accountable human, application, approval, and business purpose.
  • The article frames the real AI governance boundary as the full ecosystem of identities and authority around a model, rather than the model itself.
  • AI oversight can fail even when model accuracy, explainability, bias, security, and compliance are reviewed, because any connected identity with authority can still change system behavior or undermine integrity.
  • For generative AI, the article recommends an identity-based chain of custody that tracks who supplied and transformed data, who initiated training, who approved the model, which workload deployed it, and who can modify or retire it.
  • The article emphasizes that an attacker may not need to defeat an AI model directly if they can impersonate a trusted identity that the model, pipeline, or deployment process already accepts.

The article argues that organizations are paying attention to AI systems themselves, but often fail to track the people, accounts, applications, and automated tools that create, train, approve, change, and run them. This affects any organization using AI for things like credit decisions, medical diagnostics, hiring, industrial operations, facial recognition, cybersecurity, recommendations, logistics, robots, sensors, or autonomous vehicles. It matters because if no one can clearly connect an AI system’s actions or changes to a responsible person or trusted account, attackers or mistakes could alter data, replace models, change safety settings, steal important work, or cause harmful decisions without clear accountability.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is an opinion and best-practice perspective about the need to include identity intelligence in AI governance, rather than a report on a specific incident, vulnerability, or active threat. Ransomware Now Shows Up in Nearly Half of All Breaches: A Survival Playbook for Lean Security Teams

Ransomware now accounts for nearly half of Cyble-tracked ransomware-and-breach activity, driven by RaaS growth, double extortion, and exposed remote-access infrastructure. Lean security teams should prioritize patching internet-facing systems, locking down RMM/VPN/RDP access with MFA, deploying EDR broadly, segmenting backups, and rehearsing incident response before an attack.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Cyble’s Global Cybersecurity Report 2025 documented 5,967 ransomware attacks, a 50% year-over-year increase, and said ransomware represented 49.7% of the combined ransomware-and-breach total tracked by CRIL.
  • 02Ransomware activity remained high into 2026, including 702 attacks in March 2026 and 679 victims in January 2026, which was 30% above the 2025 monthly average.
  • 03CRIL identified 57 new ransomware groups, 27 new extortion groups, and more than 350 new ransomware strains in 2025, largely based on the MedusaLocker, Chaos, and Makop families.
  • 04The article says double extortion, where attackers encrypt systems and leak stolen data, has become standard, with some groups adding DDoS pressure or direct outreach to victims’ clients.
  • 05The article recommends that lean security teams prioritize patching internet-facing systems, securing remote-management tools, using MFA, segmenting networks, deploying EDR broadly, testing offline backups, and preparing a ransomware incident response plan in advance.

Cyble says ransomware became a dominant force in the breach landscape in 2025, with its Global Cybersecurity Report 2025 documenting 5,967 ransomware attacks, a 50% year-over-year increase. Against 6,046 data breaches and leaks in the same period, ransomware accounted for 49.7% of the combined ransomware-and-breach total tracked by CRIL. The article says activity continued into 2026, including 702 ransomware attacks in March 2026 and 679 victims in January 2026.

The article highlights that ransomware-as-a-service has lowered the skill barrier for attackers, with CRIL identifying 57 new ransomware groups, 27 new extortion groups, and more than 350 new ransomware strains in 2025. It says double extortion, where attackers encrypt systems and threaten to leak stolen data, is now standard, with some groups adding DDoS pressure or contacting victims’ clients. Lean security teams are described as especially pressured because sectors such as manufacturing and construction can face contract penalties and supply-chain disruption within days of an outage.

Cyble recommends that small teams prioritize patching internet-facing systems, securing remote-management tools, monitoring for BYOVD activity, enforcing MFA on remote access, segmenting networks, and applying least-privilege reviews. The article also says EDR coverage across every endpoint is important because groups such as Qilin use Linux-based binaries on Windows hosts and credential-harvesting toolkits. A ransomware incident response plan should include a pre-approved communication chain, tested offline backups, a ransom-payment decision framework, and enough log retention to reconstruct an intrusion timeline.

  • For lean teams, the article frames CISA KEV-listed, internet-facing systems as the highest-priority patching target because the October 2025 surge was tied to critical vulnerabilities and unpatched exposed assets.
  • The article argues that having backups no longer removes ransom pressure because data theft and leak threats are now part of standard ransomware operations.
  • Remote-management tools are singled out as a practical weak point for small teams because Qilin affiliates have abused WinSCP, AnyDesk, and ScreenConnect for lateral movement.
  • The article presents quarterly least-privilege access reviews, MFA on every remote access path, and network segmentation as achievable zero-trust steps that do not require a full enterprise-scale architecture overhaul.
  • The article emphasizes that recovery speed depends on preparation months before an incident, including validated backup integrity, restoration priorities, and rehearsed communications for customers and regulators.

The article says ransomware became a major part of the breach landscape in 2025, with Cyble tracking 5,967 ransomware attacks and continued high activity into 2026. Small security teams, especially in sectors like manufacturing and construction, are affected because outages can quickly lead to contract penalties, supply-chain disruption, and pressure to pay criminals. The broader point is that backups alone are not enough anymore because attackers often steal data too, so organizations need to prepare ahead of time with stronger access controls, monitoring, tested backups, and a response plan.

Abyssos: Technical Analysis of a New Modular RAT

Zscaler ThreatLabz analyzed Abyssos, a new actively developed modular C++ RAT that uses obfuscation, anti-analysis checks, encrypted custom TCP communications, and downloadable modules to enable credential theft, file exfiltration, VNC remote access, keylogging, and post-exploitation activity.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Zscaler ThreatLabz identified Abyssos in late June 2026 as a new modular remote administration tool written in C++.
  • 02Abyssos supports features including credential theft, file exfiltration, remote access via VNC, clipboard interception, process management, screen recording, and remote shell access.
  • 03Abyssos uses a custom TCP protocol and primarily encrypts incoming and outgoing network data with AES in GCM mode using a hardcoded 32-byte key.
  • 04ThreatLabz observed Abyssos samples using obfuscation techniques including control flow flattening, bogus control flow, constant integer encryption, and stack-based string obfuscation.
  • 05Some Abyssos samples check for hypervisors and virtualization-related processes such as VMware, KVM, Xen, VirtualBox, and QEMU tools, and terminate execution if they are detected.

Zscaler ThreatLabz identified a new malware family called Abyssos in late June 2026. Abyssos is a modular remote administration tool written in C++ and is described as being in active development. It supports capabilities including credential theft, file exfiltration, remote access through VNC, clipboard interception, process management, screen recording, and remote shell access.

The article provides a technical analysis of Abyssos version 2.4F, including its obfuscation, anti-analysis behavior, custom network protocol, and supported commands. ThreatLabz observed multiple version numbers and different obfuscation passes, including control flow flattening, bogus control flow, constant integer encryption, and stack-based string obfuscation. Some samples also check for hypervisors and virtualization-related processes such as VMware, KVM, Xen, VirtualBox, and QEMU tools, then terminate execution if they are detected.

Abyssos uses a custom TCP protocol and primarily encrypts network traffic with AES in GCM mode using a hardcoded 32-byte key. It collects host information, registers the compromised system with the command-and-control server, and then waits for commands while sending PING messages every few seconds. The malware can also download external modules for functions such as keylogging, credential recovery, cookie grabbing, domain controller discovery, vulnerability scanning, and possible privilege escalation.

  • Abyssos appears to be in active development because ThreatLabz observed multiple version numbers, different obfuscation passes, and changes in anti-analysis behavior across samples.
  • The most recent Abyssos version analyzed by ThreatLabz did not include the anti-analysis checks seen in some earlier samples, showing that those checks are not consistently present across the malware family.
  • Abyssos can hijack browser sessions by launching Chrome with debugging port 9222 and using Chrome’s Network.setCookie API to inject cookies copied into the temporary fontconfigs folder.
  • Several Abyssos capabilities depend on extra modules downloaded from the command-and-control server, with predictable temporary-file prefixes such as klog, rcv, gc, dcf, vul, and rdp.
  • Abyssos uses the --elevated command-line parameter to append _Admin to its mutex name even when the current user does not actually have administrator privileges.

Zscaler ThreatLabz found a new harmful program called Abyssos that can let someone control an infected Windows computer, steal saved information, copy files, watch the screen, record typing, and download extra parts to do more. It is being actively developed and uses tricks to hide from security tools and avoid being studied. People and organizations whose computers become infected are affected because attackers could use it to take data, hijack browser sessions, or keep remote access to the machine.

sanctions concept
Government-imposed restrictions that block or limit trade, financial dealings, or travel with targeted individuals or countries.
sanctions evasion concept
Sanctions evasion is trying to get around government restrictions placed on people, companies, or countries.
sandbox concept
A sandbox is an isolated environment used to run code more safely so it cannot easily affect the rest of the system.
sandbox analysis technique
Sandbox analysis is running a suspicious file in an isolated environment to safely watch what it does.
also: external sandbox analysis
sandbox-escape technique
A technique where malware breaks out of a restricted, isolated testing environment to attack the real underlying system.
Sandboxed execution technique
Sandboxed execution means running code inside a restricted environment so it cannot easily harm the rest of the system.
sandboxing technique
Sandboxing means running a file or program in an isolated environment so it can be observed safely without risking the real system.
Sandworm threat-actor
Sandworm is a Russian military-linked threat actor known for destructive cyberattacks and attacks on critical infrastructure.
SAP organization
SAP is a major business software company known for enterprise resource planning and other corporate systems.
SCADA concept
SCADA is a type of industrial control system used to monitor and control physical processes like power grids, water systems, and factories.
SCADA systems product
SCADA systems are industrial control systems used to monitor and control physical processes such as water, power, and manufacturing equipment.
also: SCADA interface
scammers threat-actor
Scammers are people who trick others to steal money, information, or access.
scams concept
Scams are dishonest schemes designed to trick people into giving money, information, or access.
scanner tool
A scanner is a tool that searches for information or problems automatically.
Scanners tool
Scanners are tools that check systems, networks, or websites for exposed services, weaknesses, or signs of compromise.
scanning technique
Scanning is checking computers, networks, or services to find what is reachable and what may be vulnerable.
ScarCruft threat-actor
ScarCruft is a North Korea-linked cyber-espionage threat actor tracked by security researchers.
Scattered Spider threat-actor
Scattered Spider is a cybercrime group known for social engineering, account theft, and high-profile intrusions.
scheduled-tasks
Scheduled tasks are automated jobs on a computer that attackers can abuse to run malware at specific times or after reboot.
scope concept
scope defines what access, targets, or permissions are included in a security test, login request, or authorization grant.
scopes concept
Scopes define the boundaries where a permission applies.
Scoring concept
Scoring is the practice of assigning a number or rating to show how risky, important, or suspicious something is.
screen recording technique
Screen recording is capturing video of what appears on a device's screen.
screenconnect
ScreenConnect, now ConnectWise Control, is a remote-support tool that attackers sometimes abuse for unauthorized access.
also: ConnectWise's ScreenConnect product
SD-WAN concept
SD-WAN is software-defined wide-area networking, a way to manage business network connections using centralized software controls.
SDKs tool
SDKs, or software development kits, are bundles of tools and code that help developers build apps for a platform or service.
also: analytics SDK, installation-source data from analytics SDKs
Seashell Blizzard threat-actor
Seashell Blizzard is Microsoft's name for a Russian state-linked cyber threat actor also widely associated with Sandworm.
secure-by-default development concept
Secure-by-default development means designing software so its normal settings are safe without users needing to change them.
Securing AI concept
Securing AI means protecting artificial intelligence systems from misuse, manipulation, data leaks, and unsafe behavior.
security controls concept
Security controls are safeguards, such as settings, tools, or policies, used to reduce risk.
Security Domain Secret concept
A Security Domain Secret is sensitive shared data used to protect or synchronize credentials within a security domain.
also: secret
security flaw vulnerability
A security flaw is a weakness in software, hardware, or a process that attackers could use to cause harm.
Security incident concept
A security incident is an event where systems, data, or accounts may have been attacked, exposed, or misused.
security leaders concept
Security leaders are people responsible for guiding an organization’s cybersecurity strategy and teams.
security patches concept
Security patches are software updates that fix security problems.
security products concept
Software or hardware designed to protect systems from cyber threats, like antivirus or firewalls.
security professionals concept
Security professionals are people whose job is to protect systems, data, and organizations from security threats.
Security review concept
A security review is a structured check of a system, product, or process to find and reduce security risks.
security risks concept
Security risks are possible ways that systems, data, or people could be harmed by accidents, weaknesses, or attacks.
security teams concept
Groups of professionals responsible for protecting an organization's information, systems, and networks from cyber threats.
security tools tool
Security tools are software or hardware products used to detect, prevent, investigate, or respond to cyber threats.
security updates concept
Security updates are software fixes that close vulnerabilities or improve protection against threats.
security vulnerability vulnerability
A security vulnerability is a weakness that attackers could use to break into or misuse a system.
seed phrases concept
Seed phrases are lists of words that can restore access to a cryptocurrency wallet, so stealing them can steal the funds.
self-harm concept
Self-harm means intentionally hurting oneself and can be a safety concern in online platforms and extremist or abusive communities.
self-harm activity concept
Self-harm activity refers to behavior where a person intentionally harms themselves.
Self-hosted instances concept
Self-hosted instances are copies of software that an organization runs on its own servers instead of using a vendor-hosted service.
semantic-kernel tool
Semantic Kernel is a Microsoft open-source toolkit for building applications that use AI models and plugins.
Semperis organization
Semperis is a cybersecurity company focused on identity security and Active Directory protection.
sensitive data concept
Sensitive data is information that could cause harm if exposed, such as passwords, financial details, or medical records.
sensitive information concept
Sensitive information is data that should be protected because exposing it could harm a person, company, or system.
SentinelOne organization
SentinelOne is a cybersecurity company known for endpoint detection and response products.
server infrastructure concept
Server infrastructure means the computers and supporting systems that run websites, apps, or online services.
server load balancer tool
A server load balancer spreads incoming traffic across multiple servers so no single server has to handle everything.
server-side-request-forgery vulnerability
Server-side request forgery is a vulnerability that lets an attacker make a server send requests to places the attacker should not be able to reach directly.
servers tool
Servers are computers that provide services, websites, or data to other computers over a network.
also: third-party systems
service account concept
A non-human account used by an application or service to perform automated tasks, often holding elevated privileges.
service accounts concept
Service accounts are accounts used by software or systems rather than by individual people.
Service Desk concept
A service desk is a support team that handles user requests, technical issues, and account help.
Service outage alert concept
A service outage alert is a notification that a system or online service is unavailable or not working properly.
also: notification
service provider organization
A service provider is a company or organization that delivers a service, such as hosting, software, payments, or IT support, to customers.
Session cookies concept
Session cookies are small browser-stored values that help websites remember a logged-in user during a visit.
session hijacking technique
Session hijacking is when an attacker steals or takes over a user’s logged-in web session so they can act as that user.
session tokens concept
Session tokens are temporary digital values that prove a user is already logged in to a website or service.
Severity Score concept
A severity score is a rating that helps show how serious a security flaw or incident is.
Sex Offenders Register organization
The Sex Offenders Register is a law-enforcement record of people convicted of certain sexual offenses.
sextortion technique
Sextortion is blackmail where someone threatens to share sexual images, videos, or claims unless the victim pays or does what the attacker demands.
Sexual Harm Prevention Order concept
A Sexual Harm Prevention Order is a UK court order that restricts someone to reduce the risk of sexual harm to others.
sexual images concept
Sexual images are pictures or videos with sexual content.
Shadow AI agents concept
Shadow AI agents are unauthorized or unmanaged AI agents used inside an organization without official approval or oversight.
shadow-ai
Shadow AI is the use of AI tools in an organization without official approval, visibility, or security oversight.
Shadowserver organization
Shadowserver is an internet security watchdog group that tracks exposed systems and other security data.
Shai-Hulud malware
Shai-Hulud is malware that has been described as targeting software supply chains and developer environments.
Shai-Hulud worm malware
Shai-Hulud worm is a self-spreading malware threat referenced in security reporting.
shai-hulud-chaindrop tool
shai-hulud-chaindrop is a named software package or tool referenced in security reporting.
ShareFile product
ShareFile is a file-sharing and collaboration product used by businesses to exchange documents securely.
Siemens organization
Siemens is a global technology company that makes industrial, energy, healthcare, and automation products used in many critical systems.
Siemens controllers product
Siemens controllers are industrial control devices used to operate machinery and infrastructure systems.
Siemens PLC product
A Siemens PLC is an industrial control computer made by Siemens that automates machinery or physical processes.
Siemens PLCs product
Siemens PLCs are industrial control computers made by Siemens that automate machinery and physical processes.
Sigmative API protocol
Sigmative API is an application programming interface referenced in security reporting, likely used to let software services exchange data automatically.
signed authentication material concept
Signed authentication material is login-related data protected with a digital signature so systems can verify it is genuine.
also: already generated signature, past YubiKey signatures, reusable signed assertions
sim-swapping technique
SIM swapping is a fraud technique where criminals move a victim’s phone number to a SIM card they control.
SimpleHelp product
SimpleHelp is a remote support and remote access software product used to manage computers over the internet.
Site Owner concept
Site Owner is a permission role for someone who controls settings, access, or content for a website or collaboration site.
skill concept
A voice-driven application that adds capabilities to a smart assistant like Amazon Alexa, similar to an app on a phone.
SMA 100 Series product
SMA 100 Series is SonicWall’s secure mobile access appliance line for remote access.
SMA1000 product
SMA1000 is SonicWall’s secure mobile access appliance product line for remote access.
SmarterTools SmarterMail product
SmarterTools SmarterMail is an email server and collaboration product for organizations.
SMS protocol
SMS is the standard text messaging service used on mobile phones.
Snapchat product
Snapchat is a messaging and social media app used to share photos and videos.
SOC organization
SOC stands for security operations center, a team or function that monitors and responds to security issues.
social engineering technique
Social engineering is manipulation of people into doing something or sharing information they otherwise would not.
social engineering attacks technique
Social engineering attacks are tricks that manipulate people into revealing information or doing something unsafe.
social engineering-driven attacks technique
Social engineering-driven attacks trick people into taking unsafe actions, such as revealing passwords or opening malicious files.
social media concept
Social media means online platforms where people share messages, photos, videos, and other content.
Software flaws vulnerability
Software flaws are mistakes or weaknesses in programs that can cause bugs or create security risks.
software maintainers concept
Software maintainers are the people or teams responsible for updating, fixing, and managing a software project.
software supply chain concept
The software supply chain is the set of code, libraries, tools, and vendors involved in building and delivering software.
software supply chains concept
Software supply chains are the many outside code packages, tools, services, and build steps that help create and deliver an application.
Sol API tool
Sol API is an application programming interface referenced as a named technical service or interface.
SOLICIT protocol
SOLICIT is a DHCPv6 message a device sends to find available DHCPv6 servers on the network.
Solidity Pro tool
Solidity Pro is a software extension or tool name referenced in security reporting, likely related to Solidity smart-contract development.
SonicWall organization
SonicWall is a cybersecurity vendor known for firewalls, secure remote access, and network security products.
SonicWall SMA1000 product
SonicWall SMA1000 is a secure mobile access appliance platform used for remote access to corporate networks.
Sophos organization
Sophos is a cybersecurity company that sells security products and publishes threat research.
Sopra Steria organization
Sopra Steria is a European consulting and IT services company.
SopraVPN product
SopraVPN is a VPN product or service referenced in security reporting.
Sou5 threat-actor
Sou5 is a threat-actor name referenced in security reporting.
source code concept
The human-readable code written by programmers that makes up software.
SourceForge organization
SourceForge is a website where developers can host, share, and download software projects.
South Korea National Police Agency organization
South Korea National Police Agency is South Korea's national law enforcement organization.
South Korea's National Police Agency organization
South Korea's National Police Agency is the national police organization responsible for law enforcement in South Korea.
South Korean organizations organization
South Korean organizations are companies, government agencies, or other institutions based in South Korea.
south-korea
South Korea is an East Asian country often referenced in cybersecurity stories involving technology, espionage, or regional threats.
spear-phishing technique
Spear-phishing is a targeted scam message crafted for a specific person or organization to trick them into revealing information or taking an unsafe action.
spearphishing technique
Spearphishing is a targeted scam message sent to a specific person or group to trick them into giving access or information.
spearphishing-link
A spearphishing link is a targeted phishing message that includes a malicious link tailored to a specific person or organization.
Specops Device Trust product
Specops Device Trust is a security product that helps verify whether a device should be trusted before allowing access.
Specops Password Auditor tool
Specops Password Auditor is a tool that checks an organization's passwords and password policies for weaknesses.
Specops Password Policy product
Specops Password Policy is a product that helps organizations enforce stronger password rules in Microsoft Active Directory.
Specops Software organization
A company that provides password management and authentication solutions for enterprises.
specterops organization
SpecterOps is a cybersecurity company known for identity security research and tools such as BloodHound.
Spectre vulnerability
Spectre is a class of CPU vulnerabilities that can let attackers infer sensitive data from how processors predict future work.
also: Spectre vulnerability
Spectre v2 vulnerability
Spectre v2 is a class of processor vulnerability that can trick CPUs into leaking sensitive information through speculative execution behavior.
SPF protocol
SPF is an email check that verifies whether a sending server is allowed to send email for a domain.
SplitVPN product
SplitVPN is a VPN-related product or feature name referenced in security reporting.
also: NotVPN
spoofed relay technique
A spoofed relay is a communication relay that is faked or misrepresented to make traffic appear to come from somewhere else.
spyware malware
Spyware is malicious or intrusive software that secretly monitors a person’s device, messages, location, or activity.
SQL injection technique
SQL injection is a web attack where malicious database commands are inserted into an application's input fields or requests.
also: SQLi
SQL injection vulnerability vulnerability
A SQL injection vulnerability is a weakness that lets attackers put database commands into an app to view, change, or delete data.
SSH protocol
SSH is a secure way to remotely log in to and control another computer over a network.
SSH keys protocol
SSH keys are cryptographic login credentials used to securely access remote computers and services.
SSH private keys concept
SSH private keys are secret files used to prove identity when securely logging in to servers.
Stack concept
A stack is a set of technologies, software layers, or components that work together to run an application or service.
Stale concept
Stale means something is old or not recently used and may need review, updating, or removal.
Static scanners tool
Static scanners are security tools that inspect files, links, or code without actually running them, looking for known suspicious patterns.
static scanning technique
The analysis of software source code or binaries without executing them, used to find vulnerabilities or malware.
steal and encrypt data technique
Steal and encrypt data means copying a victim's information and then locking it with encryption, a common ransomware extortion tactic.
Steam product
Steam is a popular online platform for buying, downloading, and playing video games.
Steam account product
A Steam account is a user account for Valve's Steam gaming platform.
Steam Guard codes product
Steam Guard codes are temporary security codes used for two-factor login protection on Steam accounts.
Steam hardware product
Steam hardware refers to physical gaming devices or accessories associated with Valve's Steam platform.
Stolen concept
Stolen means taken without permission, such as stolen passwords, data, or devices.
stolen credentials concept
Stolen credentials are usernames, passwords, or login tokens that attackers have obtained without permission.
stolen data concept
Stolen data is information taken without permission, often later sold, leaked, or used for extortion.
stolen files concept
Stolen files are documents or data copied or taken without permission.
stolen information concept
Stolen information is data taken without permission, such as personal details, business files, passwords, or financial records.
STOP mode concept
STOP mode is a state on some industrial controllers where the controller is not actively running its control program.
Storage bucket concept
A storage bucket is a cloud folder-like container used to store files and data objects.
Storage Zone Controllers product
Storage Zone Controllers are ShareFile components that manage where files are stored for an organization.
stored credentials concept
Stored credentials are saved usernames, passwords, tokens, or keys that let someone log in without re-entering them.
Storm-1175 threat-actor
Storm-1175 is a Microsoft-style name for a threat actor group referenced in security reporting.
also: the Storm-1175 group, the group
StormEncryptor malware
StormEncryptor is a named malware family referenced in security reporting, likely associated with file encryption or ransomware behavior.
also: a new ransomware strain
String obfuscation technique
The practice of hiding readable text inside malware code so security scanners can't easily recognize the malicious intent.
subdomain takeover technique
Subdomain takeover is when an attacker claims an abandoned service that a subdomain still points to and then controls content at that address.
supply chain concept
A supply chain is the network of vendors, software, services, and processes an organization depends on to operate.
supply chain attack technique
A supply chain attack is when attackers compromise a trusted tool, service, or distribution path to reach its users.
also: similar supply-chain attack, Another supply-chain attack
